title: Urinalysis Physical and Chemical Examination: Dipstick Principles, Interferences, and Microscopic Sediment
summary: How a urine dipstick actually works - the chemistry behind each pad, the interferences that produce false results, the meaning of specific gravity and pH, and a systematic approach to recognizing sediment elements from cells to casts to crystals, with disciplined reporting language.
objectives: Explain the reagent chemistry of each major dipstick pad and name its principal interferences.
Compare refractometer, reagent strip, and osmolality measurements of urine concentration and their limitations.
Identify the major sediment elements - cells, casts, crystals, and contaminants - and their clinical significance.
Report urinalysis findings with appropriate correlation language and avoid overinterpreting single abnormal findings.

highYield: The protein pad uses the protein error of indicators: a pH-sensitive dye changes color in the presence of protein, mostly albumin; it is much less sensitive to globulins and Bence Jones protein.
Nitrite positivity requires nitrate-reducing Gram-negative organisms and sufficient bladder dwell time (roughly 4 hours or more); a negative nitrite does not exclude infection.
Leukocyte esterase detects esterase from intact or lysed granulocytes and is a screening marker for pyuria and many urinary tract infections.
Ascorbic acid (vitamin C) can cause false-negative results for blood, glucose, nitrite, and bilirubin on peroxidase-based pads.
Red blood cell casts and muddy brown granular casts localize pathology to the nephron and must always be reported with urgency.

quickReview.mnemonic: Cast legend: 'RBC cast = renal bleeding (glomerulus), WBC cast = white cell war (pyelonephritis), granular muddy brown = tubular injury, waxy = chronic failure, hyaline = just concentrated protein soup.'

deepStudy.introduction: Urinalysis is the oldest clinical laboratory test and still one of the most informative, provided each finding is interpreted as part of a triad: physical examination (color, clarity, specific gravity, pH), chemical screening (dipstick), and microscopic sediment. The dipstick is a set of miniaturized chemical reactions on plastic pads, each with a defined principle and a defined set of lies - interferents that flip results positive or negative. The microscope then confirms or refutes the chemistry: blood on dipstick without intact red cells suggests myoglobin or hemoglobin or a chemical false positive; protein on dipstick without sediment findings may be orthostatic or falsely elevated by alkaline pH. This lesson covers the concentration and pH measurements, walks pad by pad through the chemistry and its interference, and finishes with a disciplined approach to sediment recognition and reporting. Any reference interval quoted here (for example, typical random urine specific gravity ranges) is illustrative of textbook descriptions only and varies by laboratory, method, population, age, and hydration; the performing laboratory's own intervals govern reporting.

sections.heading: Color, clarity, specific gravity, and pH
sections.body: Physical examination begins with color and clarity recorded objectively - pale, yellow, amber, red, brown, cloudy - because color drives the differential (red suggests hematuria, myoglobin, porphyrins, beets, or drugs; dark brown suggests bilirubin or old blood). Specific gravity estimates urine concentrating ability; refractometry measures the refractive index and is influenced by protein and glucose, while the dipstick estimates it by polyelectrolyte ion exchange that releases hydrogen ions proportional to ionic concentration, so it tracks solutes rather than macromolecules and can read falsely low in alkaline urine. Osmolality by freezing-point depression is the true measure of particle concentration but is not practical for every specimen. Typical textbook intervals for random urine specific gravity run roughly from about 1.005 to 1.030, but these vary by laboratory, method, and hydration status and must be verified locally. Urine pH (typically mildly acidic, often around 5 to 7 in random specimens) reflects diet, acid-base status, and bacterial urease activity; alkaline urine in a fresh specimen suggests a urea-splitting organism or a vegetarian diet, and a pH above 7.5 can predispose to struvite crystal formation and to false-positive protein readings. Record pH and specific gravity with every chemical screen because both modify interpretation of the other pads.

sections.heading: Dipstick pad chemistry and the interference table
sections.body: Each pad is a small essay in applied chemistry. The protein pad exploits the protein error of indicators: at a fixed pH, protein binds dye and shifts its color, and the reaction is far more sensitive to albumin than to globulins or light chains, so negative dipstick protein does not exclude Bence Jones proteinuria; alkaline urine and quaternary ammonium compounds can produce false positives. The glucose pad uses glucose oxidase specific for beta-D-glucose with a peroxidase-linked color reaction, making oxidizing contaminants (bleach) false positives and ascorbic acid, high specific gravity, and ketones false negatives. The blood pad detects pseudoperoxidase activity of hemoglobin and myoglobin, lysing red cells and turning the pad green; it cannot distinguish intact erythrocytes from free hemoglobin or myoglobin, so microscopy is the arbiter. The nitrite pad waits for bacterial nitrate reduction to nitrite and then couples with Griess reagent, demanding both nitrate-reducing Gram-negative organisms and adequate bladder dwell time - which is why a negative nitrite never rules out infection and why Enterococcus and staphylococci (poor nitrate reducers) are missed. Leukocyte esterase catches granulocyte esterase and is skewed by heavy protein or glucose and by organisms that do not provoke pyuria. The ketone pad (sodium nitroprusside) reacts with acetoacetate and acetone, not beta-hydroxybutyrate, the dominant ketone in diabetic ketoacidosis, so early ketoacidosis can read negative. Bilirubin uses the diazo reaction and fades with light exposure. Ascorbic acid deserves its own paragraph: at high concentrations it scavenges peroxidase radicals and causes false-negative blood, glucose, nitrite, and bilirubin results - a classic vignette detail.

sections.heading: Microscopic sediment: cells, casts, and contaminants
sections.body: Centrifuged urine sediment read under reduced light is where anatomy meets pathology. Erythrocytes may be isomorphic (suggesting lower tract source) or dysmorphic with acanthocytes (suggesting glomerular bleeding), and yeast or crystals can masquerade as red cells - yeast bud and do not lyse in acetic acid, crystals are refractile and geometric. Leukocytes are usually neutrophils; clumps signal inflammation, but vaginal contamination brings squamous epithelial cells and mucus, and any specimen with many squamous cells should be reported as contaminated rather than quantified. Renal tubular epithelial cells are round with large nuclei and signal tubular injury. Casts are protein gels formed in the distal tubule and carry whatever lies within: hyaline casts (pure Tamm-Horsfall protein, seen in concentrated urine or after exercise), granular casts (degenerating cellular debris), muddy brown granular casts (acute tubular injury), waxy casts (advanced chronic kidney disease), red blood cell casts (glomerulonephritis - always significant), white blood cell casts (pyelonephritis or interstitial nephritis), and fatty casts with oval fat bodies (nephrotic syndrome). Crystals depend on pH and concentration: calcium oxalate envelope-shaped (and dumbbell in acidic urine), uric acid diamond or rosette shapes, triple phosphate coffin-lid crystals in alkaline urine (struvite risk), ammonium biurate thorn-apple forms in old or refrigerated specimens, cystine hexagonal plates (inherited defect), and leucine and tyrosine crystals in severe liver disease. Report casts with their type and confirm at least two per low-power field when significance is claimed, per your laboratory's procedure.

sections.heading: Correlation and reporting discipline
sections.body: The value of urinalysis is in the pattern. Dipstick blood positive with intact red cells confirms hematuria; dipstick blood positive with no cells prompts myoglobin consideration (rhabdomyolysis, strenuous exercise) or chemical interference. Dipstick protein positive with a bland sediment suggests overflow (paraprotein), orthostatic, or tubular proteinuria and needs quantitation (urine protein-to-creatinine ratio or 24-hour collection) rather than panic. Nitrite positive with leukocyte esterase positive strongly supports urinary tract infection and should be reflexed to culture per protocol; nitrite negative with esterase positive can be any pyuria, including infection with non-nitrate reducers. Alkaline pH plus triple phosphate crystals plus symptoms suggests urea-splitting infection with struvite risk. Concentrated specific gravity plus hyaline casts is a physiologic finding, not disease. Always document specimen type (clean-catch, catheter, suprapubic), collection time, and any obvious contamination or delay, because preanalytic facts change meaning. When chemical and microscopic findings disagree, repeat the dipstick on a fresh specimen and inspect for interferents before releasing the result, and attach comments such as ascorbic acid interference, contaminated specimen, or correlation with culture recommended as your procedure allows. Reference intervals for formed elements vary by laboratory, method, and population and must be verified locally before use in decision limits.

deepStudy.clinicalSignificance: Urinalysis screens for urinary tract infection, glomerular and tubular disease, diabetes, liver disease, and metabolic disorders. Red blood cell casts change the workup to nephrology; white blood cell casts signal pyelonephritis rather than cystitis; muddy brown granular casts define acute tubular injury. Dipstick glucose with ketones and high specific gravity in an acid urine is the urinalysis signature of uncontrolled diabetes. Bilirubinuria precedes jaundice in biliary obstruction. Contaminated specimens waste cultures and antibiotics, so honest reporting of squamous epithelial cells prevents overtreatment. In every case, the physical, chemical, and microscopic legs must agree before the report is released, and discordance is itself a reportable finding.
deepStudy.labInterpretation: Report color and clarity in words, specific gravity and pH as numbers with the method (refractometer versus reagent strip), and chemical results in the manufacturer's categories (negative, trace, 1+, 2+, 3+, 4+ for protein; negative to 3+ for others as per your strip's chart). Microscopic results should be quantified per your laboratory's scheme (for example, cells per high-power field, casts per low-power field) with the centrifugation and volume conditions stated. Comment on discordance: for example, dipstick 2+ protein with negative sediment still requires quantitation; blood positive with no red cells suggests myoglobin or interferent. State contamination (many squamous epithelial cells), delay, or refrigeration effects when they limit interpretation. All numeric intervals - specific gravity, pH, cell counts - carry the standing caveat that intervals vary by laboratory, method, population, age, and collection conditions, and local verified intervals govern the report.

examTraps: A negative nitrite does not exclude urinary tract infection - dwell time and organism nitrate reduction both matter, and Enterococcus does not reduce nitrate well.
Ascorbic acid causes false-negative blood, glucose, nitrite, and bilirubin; if the clinical picture disagrees, ask about vitamin C intake and rerun with a method free of that interference.
The protein pad detects albumin preferentially; negative dipstick protein never excludes Bence Jones protein or immunoglobulin light chains.
Squamous epithelial cells mean contamination, not pyuria - reporting neutrophil quantification from such a specimen misleads treatment.

memoryHooks.text: For dipstick interferents: 'Vitamin C erases (blood, glucose, nitrite, bilirubin false negatives); alkaline urine inflates (protein false positive); bleach inflates (blood and glucose false positive).'
memoryHooks.funny: Mimi: 'Ang vitamin C, parang ghostwriter - pinapabura ang mga positive results! Ang alkaline urine naman, drama queen - lahat ng protein, positive daw.'

memoryHooks.text: RBC cast = glomerulus bleeding. WBC cast = infection upstream (pyelonephritis). Muddy brown = tubular ruin.
memoryHooks.funny: Casts sa urine = may galing sa taas ng daan. Pag may RBC cast, seryoso yan - wag papakalmahin, urgent yan!
